speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Good afternoon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: My colleagues and I remain squarely focused on achieving our dual-mandate goals of maximum employment and stable prices for the benefit of the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The economy is strong overall and has made significant progress toward our goals over the past two years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Labor market conditions are solid, and inflation has moved closer to our 2 percent longer-run goal, though it remains somewhat elevated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In support of our goals, today the Federal Open Market Committee decided to leave our policy interest rate unchanged.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We also made the technical decision to slow the pace of decline in the size of our balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’ll have more to say about these decisions after briefly reviewing economic developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Economic activity continued to expand at a solid pace in the fourth quarter of last year, with GDP rising at 2.3 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Recent indications, however, point to a moderation in consumer spending following the rapid growth seen over the second half of 2024.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Surveys of households and businesses point to heightened uncertainty about the economic outlook.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It remains to be seen how these developments might affect future spending and investment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In our Summary of Economic Projections, the median participant projects GDP to rise 1.7 percent this year, somewhat lower than projected in December, and to rise a bit below 2 percent over the next two years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In the labor market, conditions remain solid.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Payroll job gains averaged 200,000 per month over the past three months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The unemployment rate, at 4.1 percent, remains low and has held in a narrow range for the past year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The jobs-to-workers gap has held steady for several months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Wages are growing faster than inflation and at a more sustainable pace than earlier in the pandemic recovery.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Overall, a wide set of indicators suggests that conditions in the labor market are broadly in balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The labor market is not a source of significant inflationary pressures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The median projection for the unemployment rate in the SEP is 4.4 percent at the end of this year and 4.3 percent over the next two years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation has eased significantly over the past two years but remains somewhat elevated relative to our 2 percent longer-run goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Estimates based on the consumer price index and other data indicate that total PCE prices rose 2.5 percent over the 12 months ending in February and that, excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core PCE prices rose 2.8 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Some near-term measures of inflation expectations have recently moved up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We see this in both market- and survey-based measures, and survey respondents, both consumers and businesses, are mentioning tariffs as a driving factor.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Beyond the next year or so, however, most measures of longer-term expectations remain consistent with our 2 percent inflation goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The median projection in the SEP for total PCE inflation is 2.7 percent this year and 2.2 percent next year, a little higher than projected in December.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In 2027, the median projection is at our 2 percent objective.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our monetary policy actions are guided by our dual mandate to promote maximum employment and stable prices for the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At today’s meeting, the Committee decided to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 4¼ to 4½ percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Looking ahead, the new Administration is in the process of implementing significant policy changes in four distinct areas: trade, immigration, fiscal policy, and regulation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It is the net effect of these policy changes that will matter for the economy and for the path of monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: While there have been recent developments in some of these areas, especially trade policy, uncertainty around the changes and their effects on the economic outlook is high.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As we parse the incoming information, we’re focused on separating the signal from the noise as the outlook evolves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As we say in our statement, in considering the extent and timing of additional adjustments to the target range for the federal funds rate, the Committee will assess incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We do not need to be in a hurry to adjust our policy stance, and we are well positioned to wait for greater clarity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In our SEP, FOMC participants wrote down their individual assessments of an appropriate path for the federal funds rate, based on what each participant judges to be the most likely scenario going forward—an admittedly challenging exercise at this time in light of considerable uncertainty.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The median participant projects that the appropriate level of the federal funds rate will be 3.9 percent at the end of this year and 3.4 percent at the end of next year, unchanged from December.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: While these individual forecasts are always subject to uncertainty, as I noted, uncertainty today is unusually elevated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, of course, these projections are not a Committee plan or a decision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Policy is not on a preset course.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As the economy evolves, we will adjust our policy stance in a manner that best promotes our maximum-employment and price-stability goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If the economy remains strong and inflation does not continue to move sustainably toward 2 percent, we can maintain policy restraint for longer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If the labor market were to weaken unexpectedly or inflation were to fall more quickly than anticipated, we can ease policy accordingly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our current policy stance is well positioned to deal with the risks and uncertainties that we face in pursuing both sides of our dual mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At today’s meeting, we also decided to slow the pace of decline in our balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Since we began balance sheet runoff, our securities holdings have declined by more than $2 trillion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: While market indicators continue to suggest that the quantity of reserves remains abundant, we have seen some signs of increased tightness in money markets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Beginning in April, the monthly cap on Treasury redemptions will be lowered from $25 billion to $5 billion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Consistent with the Committee’s intention to hold primarily Treasury securities in the longer run, we are leaving the cap on agency securities unchanged.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This action has no implications for our intended stance of monetary policy and should not affect the size of our balance sheet over the medium term.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The Committee also continued its discussions as part of our five-year review of our monetary policy framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At this meeting, we focused on labor market dynamics and our maximum-employment goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As we have indicated, our review will include outreach and public events involving a wide range of parties, including Fed Listens events around the country and a research conference in May.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Throughout this process, we will be open to new ideas and critical feedback, and we will take on board lessons of the last five years in determining our findings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We intend to wrap up the review by late summer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The Fed has been assigned two goals for monetary policy: maximum employment and stable prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We remain committed to supporting maximum employment, bringing inflation sustainably to our 2 percent goal, and keeping longer-term inflation expectations well anchored.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our success in delivering on these goals matters to all Americans.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We understand that our actions affect communities, families, and businesses across the country.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Everything we do is in service to our public mission.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We at the Fed will do everything we can to achieve our maximum-employment and price-stability goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I will look forward to your questions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So let me say that it is going to be very difficult to have a precise assessment of how much of inflation is coming from tariffs and from, from other—and that’s already the case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You may have seen that goods inflation moved up pretty significantly in the first two months of the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Trying to track that back to actual tariff increases, given what was tariffed and what was not—very, very challenging.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So some of it—the, the answer is clearly some of it—a good part of it is, is coming from tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we’ll be—we’ll be working, and so will other forecasters, to try to find the best possible way to separate nontariff inflation from tariff inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In terms of the, the—your, your sort of looking-through question, too soon to say about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As, as I’ve mentioned, it, it can be the case that it’s appropriate sometimes to look through inflation if it’s going to go away quickly without action by, by us, if it’s transitory.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that can be the case in the case of, of tariff inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think that would depend on the, the tariff inflation moving through fairly quickly and would depend critically, as well, on inflation expectations being well anchored—longer-term inflation expectations being well anchored.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think—I think that’s kind of the base case, but, as I said, it’s—we really can’t know that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re going to have to see how things actually, actually work out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the fact that there wasn’t much change—I think that’s, that’s partly because, you know, you see—you see weaker growth but higher inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They kind of offset.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And also, frankly, a little bit of inertia when it—when it comes to changing something in this highly uncertain environment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, you’re—you, you know, I think there is a level of inertia where you just say, “Maybe I’ll stay where I am.” MICHELLE SMITH.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Colby.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So our inflation expectations—of course, we do monitor inflation expectations very, very carefully—basically, every source we can find, and, you know—short-term, long-term, households, businesses, forecasters, market-based.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think the picture, broadly, is this: You do see increases widely in short-term inflation expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And people who fill out surveys and answer, you know, questionnaires are pointing to tariffs about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you look—in the survey world, if you look a little further out, you, you really—you really don’t see much in the way of an increased longer-term inflation—inflation expectations are mostly well anchored, if you look at the [series maintained by the Federal Reserve Bank of] New York, for example.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Then you have market based, and it’s the same pattern.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, people and markets are pricing in and, and breakevens, some higher inflation over the next year must be related to tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We know from the surveys.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But if you look out five years or five-year, five-year forward, you’ll see that breakevens have—are either flat or, actually, slightly down in the case of a longer-term one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we look at that, and we will be watching all of it very, very carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We do not take anything for granted.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s at the very heart of our framework: anchored inflation expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But what—that’s what you see right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So let’s start with the hard data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we, we do see pretty solid hard data still.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So growth looks like it’s maybe moderating a bit, consumer spending moderating a bit, but still at a solid pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Unemployment’s 4.1 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Job creation, most recently, has been at a healthy level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation has started to move up now, we think partly in response to tariffs, and there may be a delay in further progress over the course of this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s the hard data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Overall, it’s a solid picture.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The, the survey data, [in the case of] both household and businesses, show significant rise in uncertainty and significant concerns about downside risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s—that is the question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As I mentioned the other day, as you pointed out, the relationship between survey data and actual economic activity hasn’t been very tight.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There have been plenty of times where people are saying very down—downbeat things about the economy and then going out and buying a new car.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we don’t know that that will be the case here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We will be watching very carefully for signs of weakness in the real data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Of course we will.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I, I—you know, given where we are, we think our policy’s in a good place to react to, to what comes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we think that the right thing to do is, is to wait here for, you know, for greater clarity about, about what, what the economy’s doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I, I do like that definition a lot.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In fact, I used it at the recent conference where I spoke.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think a world where, where people can make their daily economic decisions, and businesses, and they’re not having to think about the possibility of significantly high inflation—we know inflation will bounce around.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s, that is price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, I think we were getting closer and closer to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I wouldn’t say we were at that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation was running around 2½ percent for some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I do think with the arrival of, of the tariff inflation, further progress may be delayed, if the SEP doesn’t really show further downward progress on inflation this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that, that’s really due to the tariffs coming in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, delayed, but if you look at our forecast, we do see ourselves getting back into the low 2s in ’26 and then down to 2 [percent] by ’27—of course, highly uncertain.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I see progress having, having been made toward that, and then progress in the future.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think that progress is probably delayed for the time being.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, again, people wrote down two cuts the last time, and they look at—they look at the—you know, the—and they wrote down, you know, meaningful decline in growth out from 2.1 to 1.7 in 2025, a tick up in the unemployment rate, so not much there, but core inflation up by three-tenths.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so those two kind of—those kind of balance each other out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So people—not everybody, but, on balance, people wrote down similar numbers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The changes aren’t that big.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The other—the other factor, though, as I mentioned, is just really high uncertainty.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, it’s just—it’s really hard to know how this is going to work out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, again, we think our policy’s in a good place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We think it’s a good place where we can move in the direction that—where we need to.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But in the meantime, we, we—it’s, it’s really appropriate to wait for further clarity, and, of course, you know, the costs of doing that, given that the economy is still solid, are very low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah, so that’s a feature of the—has been for some time, a feature of this labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You have pretty high participation, accounting for aging.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You’ve got wages that are consistent with 2 percent inflation, assuming that we’re going to keep getting, you know, relatively high productivity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve got unemployment, you know, pretty close to its natural level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But job—the hiring rate is quite low, but so is the layoff rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the, the—you look at initial claims or layoffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you’re not seeing people losing their jobs, but you’re seeing that people who don’t have a job having to wait longer and longer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If we were to see a meaningful increase in layoffs, then that would probably translate fairly quickly into unemployment, because people are—you know, it’s, it’s not a—it’s not a big hiring market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve been watching that, and it’s just not in the data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It hasn’t happened.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What we’ve had is, is a low-firing, low-hiring situation, and it seems to be in balance now for, you know, for the last six, seven, eight months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s where we are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There’s healthy levels of job creation, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, overall, it’s a labor market that’s in balance, and, you know, we, we watch it very carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I, you know, only in a—kind of an early way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, for example, the, the layoffs that are happening here are, you know, they’re certainly meaningful to the people involved, and they may be meaningful to a particular neighborhood or region or area, but at the national level, they’re not—they’re not significant yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we don’t know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t know what—where that—how far that will go.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ll, we’ll find out much more.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mentioned that—you, you saw it—we’ve had two, two very strong goods inflation readings in the last two months, which is very unexpected, and, I think, hard to trace it to specific tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it must have—it must have something to do with—it’s either noise and it’ll come back, and that—that’s very possible, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But if it is persistent, then it must be to do with, you know, people buying ahead of tariffs, or raising prices ahead of tariffs, and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That—those kinds of things happen, and they’re very, very hard to capture because so much of it is indirect.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: A great example is there—washing machines were tariffed in the last, last round of tariffs, and prices went up, but prices also went up on, on dryers, which were not tariffed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the manufacturers just, you know, they just kind of followed the crowd and, and raised it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So things happen very indirectly, and so there’ll be a lot of work done in the coming months to, to try to trace all that through.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, ultimately, though, it’s too soon to be seeing significant effects in economic data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: When you say “last time,” are you talking about the last— CRAIG TORRES.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Pandemic, yes—during the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You could have been talking about the last time there were tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In which case, the inflation was, was transitory.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: No—of course, we’re well aware of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, it’s, it’s still the truth, if, if there’s an inflationary impulse that’s going to go away on its own, it’s not the right policy to, to tighten policy, because by the time you have your effect, you’re—you know, you’re—an effect that by—by design, you are lowering economic activity and employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And if that’s not necessary, you don’t want to do it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In real time, as we know, it’s hard to make that judgment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So—and, and we’re well aware, you know, of what happened, obviously, with, with the pandemic inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, I mean, we have to look at this as a—as a different situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There’s, there are differences and similarities.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, it’s a different time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we haven’t had real price stability fully reestablished yet, and we have to keep that in mind.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, we also have—we hear that people are very reluctant to take on—to, you know, to, to allow prices to go up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At the same time, we hear that businesses are intending to pass many of these prices through.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s hard to say how this is going to work out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We have maximum employment and price stability, and we have to balance those.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we have, actually have a provision in our—in our consensus statement that says what we should do in that case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s a very challenging, you know, situation for, for any central bank, and certainly for us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so, what we say that we’ll do is, we’ll, we’ll look how far each of those two goals is—each of those two measures is from its goal, and then we’ll ask how long we think it might take to get back to the goal for each of them, and we’ll make a judgment, because our, you know, our tools work in one direction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re either tightening or loosening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s a very challenging situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Let me say, we don’t have that situation right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s not what the—that’s not where the economy is at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s also not where the forecast is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t know any mainstream forecast that really shows significant problems like that, so— STEVE LIESMAN.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, just to follow up, yesterday the UCLA Anderson Forecast said there’s—a high probability of a recession.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, there’s always an unconditional probability—possibility of, of a recession.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It might be broadly in the range of one in four at any time, if you look back through, through the years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It—there could be, within 12 months, a one in four chance of a recession.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the question is, is whether that—whether this current situation, those possibilities are elevated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I will say this: We don’t—we don’t make such a forecast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you look at outside forecasts, forecasters have, have generally raised—a number of them have raised their possibility of a—of a recession somewhat, but still at relatively moderate levels—you know, still in the region of, of the traditional, because they were extremely low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you go back two months, people were saying that the, the likelihood of a recession was extremely low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, has moved up, but it’s not high.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think I, I did answer that question in this very room some time ago, and I, I [have] no desire to change that answer and have nothing new for you on that today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I, I mentioned it back then, but in no way did I place a huge weight on it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think it, it—that was an ex post story, but it wasn’t the case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That was a preliminary reading, and so is this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it’s also—this is—that, that Michigan, the one you’re referring to, the longer-term thing—you know, we look at it, and we don’t dismiss data that we don’t like.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We, we force ourselves to look at it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it is an outlier compared to market-based and compared to other survey-based assessments of longer-run inflation expectations, so we’ve got to keep that in mind.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I, I—again, I, I would just say, we look at—we look at all of them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that one—that one’s kind of an outlier, but, you know, nonetheless, we, we take notice of it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah, look, we’re, we’re aware of the—we’re well aware of how things are going to evolve and the time frames and all that, and, you know, we will—we will use our tools to foster achievement of our goals to the—to the best we can.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, of course, we’re going to try to be timely with that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: For right now, the hard data are pretty solid.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We, we are obviously aware of the soft sentiment data and high uncertainty, and we’re watching that carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we think it’s a, a good time for us to wait for further clarity before we consider adjusting our, our policy stance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yes, I think we will.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I just—it’s hard to say when that will be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we’re—these decisions are going to be made, and they’re going to be implemented, and then we’ll know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At that point, we’ll know what the decisions are, and we’ll have to make assessments then about their, their implications for the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Those things will happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: A lot of them will happen over the course of, you know, in coming months, certainly over the course of this year, and we’ll be adapting as we go.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So when we say “separating the signal from the noise,” that’s just a way of saying that things are highly uncertain and that, you know, you’re reading about developments—the news is full of developments of tariffs being put on and taken off and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s—some of that is noise in the sense that it’s, it’s not really telling you anything.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You’re trying to extract a signal from that, and the signal is what’s going to be the effect on economic activity, on inflation, on employment, and all those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s, that’s sort of a, a special case of that—of, you know, with the idea being—and I think—do think that the first two months of this year are a great example.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You’ve got high readings for goods inflation after a string of readings that averaged close to zero, and you have to ask—it’s coming during tariffs, but, you know, you—it’s very hard to, actually, scientifically go back and match up those increases and say, “Yes, I can prove that that’s from tariffs.” But it kind of has to be, to some extent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Plus, noise.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There can be idiosyncratic readings in various categories, which will shortly reverse, and that, that happens, too, and that could be a big piece of it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, I think we’ll know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In a couple of months, we’ll know whether those were—you know, where that really was from.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it’s a—that’s another case where I think it’s going to be very, very challenging to unpack the inflation that we see over the course of this year and be able to say with confidence how much of that came from inflation and how much of it—sorry, from tariffs—and how much of it didn’t.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But that’s what we’ll be doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ll be doing that, and so will everybody else, and we’ll all be trying very hard to, to make that assessment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, I, I’m sure we will make a lot of progress on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we already have.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it, it’s going to be a challenge.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, it would depend on what we’re talking about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, obviously, you’re looking for direct evidence that, that particular pieces of, of inflation are, are—or are clearly not—caused by tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: For example, something that was, you know, in the service sector that was far away from anything that’s tariffed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You, you might think, okay, well that is—like, frankly, housing services inflation—which, which, by the way, has been behaving well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know—which, for, for some time, was kind of our problem.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Now it’s been—it’s slow, but it’s definitely, you know, moving down in a—in a very good way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s more now with goods and, to some extent, with, with nonhousing services inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Okay, so a couple things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The grocery bill is about, about past inflation, really.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There was inflation in ’21, ’22, and ’23, and prices went up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The current level—it’s not the change in prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s, they’re unhappy—and, and they’re not wrong to be unhappy—that prices went up quite a bit, and they’re paying a lot for those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s—I think that is the fundamental fact and has been for a long time—a couple years—why people are unhappy with the—with the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not that the economy’s not growing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not that inflation’s really high.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not that unemployment is high.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s none of those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We have, you know, 4.1 percent unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve got 2 percent growth, and, you know, it’s, it’s a pretty good economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But people are unhappy because of the price level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, and I do—we completely understand and accept that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I, I think if you—yeah, I mean, remember, we came into this with—at the December meeting, and the median was two cuts, the median was.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so you come in, and you see, broadly speaking, weaker growth but higher inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And they kind of balance each other out, so you think—and, and unemployment is really, really only, only a one-tenth change.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s—there’s just not a big change in the forecast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There really isn’t.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So they cancel each other out, and people just said, “Okay, I’m going to stay here.” But the second factor is, it’s so highly uncertain.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Is just—you know, we’re sitting here thinking—and we, we obviously are in, in touch with businesses and households all over the country.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We have an extraordinary network of contacts that come in through the Reserve Banks and put it in the Beige Book—and also through contacts at the Board.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we get all that, and we, we do understand that sentiment has fallen off pretty sharply, but economic activity has not yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so we’re watching carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I would tell people that the economy seems to be— seems to be healthy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We understand that, that sentiment is, is quite negative at this time, and that probably has to do with, you know, turmoil at the beginning of an Administration.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s making, you know, big changes in, in areas of policy, and that’s probably part of it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I do think the underlying unhappiness people have about the economy, though, is more—is more about the price level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah, so, in the SEP, you’ll see that there’s not further progress on core inflation this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re kind of side flatlining, going sideways.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t ask people to say—to write down how much of this is from tariffs and how much of it is not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But some of it is from tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We know that tariffs are coming, and we know that they’re probably already—all, all forecasters have tariff inflation affecting core PCE inflation [and] core CPI inflation this year, without exception.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’m not aware of an exception.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s in there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I can’t tell you how much of that it is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In terms of the balance sheet—so, yeah, we—I think—I guess the way I’d say it is, you know, it was the flows in and out of the, the TGA that got us thinking about it, but as we, you know, as we thought about it, we really came to the view that this was a good time to, to make the move that we made.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Whenever it was, we, we lowered the pace of QT, and we’re just going to do that again.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re going to cut it roughly in half.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s going—it’s going to be slower for longer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And people really liked that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: People thought, “That’s, that’s a good idea.” You know, it’s like a plane.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You can think of it like a plane coming in for a landing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As we get closer and we—by the way, we still think that reserves are abundant, although you begin to see some of the—some of the things we look at begin to react a little bit, but we still think that they’re abundant.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, of course, now, the TGA is emptying out, so reserves are, are higher now, so you can’t really see the underlying signal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we came around to the view, and, and it had a lot of appeal, and so we did it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It really—it has no implications at all for monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It has no implications at all for the ultimate size of the balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It isn’t sending a signal in any hidden way that you can try to tease out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s just not there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re, we’re basically—it’s very consistent with our plans and our practices that we’ve published and that we’ve followed since we began this—what is a very successful, you know, rundown of the balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Again, [this is] the second time that we’ve slowed the pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’ve said that we would stop when we were somewhat above the level [of reserves] we judge as ample.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, clearly, we’re not at that level yet, but we’re going to be approaching it more slowly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s a commonsense kind of a—kind of a thing, and it had—it had pretty broad appeal, I will say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So when we—when we talk about inflation expectations being well anchored, we’re talking about longer-run inflation expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And they really haven’t moved much, I mean, if at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There, there’s one reading that everyone’s focusing on that’s higher, but the other survey readings and the market-based readings all show relatively, you know, well-anchored inflation expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You would expect that expectations of inflation over the course of a year would move around, because conditions change, and in this case, we have tariffs coming in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t know how big, what’s—there’s so many things we don’t know, but we kind of know there are going to be tariffs, and they tend to bring growth down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They tend to bring inflation up at the—in the first instance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, so I would say, you, you know, I’m not dismissing what we’re seeing in short-term inflation expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We, as I mentioned, follow that very carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But when we say expectations are well anchored, we’re really looking at, you know, longer term, five year and out, and there’s really no story to tell five years and out, either in market based or, or in surveys.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we keep—we’ll watch it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, we’re not, you know, we’re, we’re not going to miss any evidence that longer-term or medium-term inflation expectations are, are moving.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that, that has been the case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We talked about that over the course of the last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There were—there were some good number of months and times when a lot of the job creation was, was concentrated in, you know, educational institutions, health care, state governments, things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There were also times when private-sector job growth has been moving, moving in a healthy frame—and they’re all—they’re all jobs, but—and remember, we’re, you know, we’re at very low unemployment for, you know, for, for quite a time now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I, I think it’s a good labor market, but it’s—look, it’s something that we monitor carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: From our standpoint, employment is employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I, you know—the, the elected government is entitled to have—you know, we, we don’t have policies that address different kinds of employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, but the elected government has a—has a different role, and they can—they, they can have those.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think tapering it—I, I don’t know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There’s no plan to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, at a certain point, we’ll stop runoff.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we may or may not stop MBS runoff, though, because, you know, we can—we can—we, we want to stop runoff in net at some point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We haven’t made any decisions about that, but, you know, we, we want the—we want the MBS to roll off our balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We really, strongly desire that, so—but we haven’t made any decisions about that, you know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We, we will—we—I think we’d, we’d look carefully at letting that keep going, but hold the overall size of the balance sheet in, you know, constant, at some point—a point that we’re not at yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’m confident that we’re well positioned in the sense that we’re, we’re well positioned to move in the direction we’ll need to move.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I, I mean, I, I don’t know anyone who has a lot of confidence in their forecast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, the point is, we are—we are at, you know, we’re at a place where we can cut or we—or we can hold what is a clearly a restrictive stance of policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s what I mean.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I, I mean, I think we’re—that’s well positioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Forecasting right now, it’s—you know, forecasting is always very, very hard, and in the current situation, I just think it’s—uncertainty is, you know, remarkably high.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I, like, I, I think we’re not going to be in any hurry to move.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, as I mentioned, I think we’re, we’re well positioned to wait for further clarity, and not in any hurry.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Actually, it does not mean either of those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, sometimes with language they—it, it lives its, its useful life, and then we take it off, and we—and, and that was the case there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There’s really not meant to be any signal here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Over the past year, you know, conveying this sense of the balance of risks was important that they be in balance or close to being in balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That was useful as we approach liftoff, if you remember.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we’re past that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Or, I’m sorry, no—beginning, beginning to cut.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we just—so we just took it out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I, I actually would say that the more important thing now about risks—and this is in, in pages like 10, 11, 12 of the SEP—if you look, participants widely raised their estimate of, of the risks to our—of uncertainty, but also of the risks to growth in our employment and inflation mandates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s, that’s a more salient point now than whether they’re—whether they’re in balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So financial conditions matter to us because, you know, financial conditions are the main channel to the real economy through which our policy has its effect.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, so they’re important.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But what matters from, from a Fed standpoint for the macroeconomy is material changes to overall financial conditions that are persistent, that last for a while—long enough to actually affect economic activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s what we’re looking for.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I, I’m not going to opine on the appropriate level of any market—equity, debt, commodities, or anything like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I would just point you to the—to the bigger picture again.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, the, the real economy, the, the hard data are still in, in reasonably good shape.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s the soft data—it’s the surveys that are showing, you know, significant concerns, downside risks, and those kind of things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t dismiss that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re watching it carefully, but, you know, we, we don’t want to get ahead of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we, we want to focus on the hard data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This—if it’s—if that’s going to affect the hard data, we should know it very quickly, and, and, of course, we’ll, we’ll understand that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But you don’t see that yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, fortunately, we’re in a situation where we have seen inflation move down from, you know, higher levels to pretty close to 2 percent, while the unemployment rate has remained very consistent with full employment, 4.1 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we now have inflation coming in from an exogenous source, but the underlying inflationary picture before that was, you know, basically 2½ percent inflation, I would say, and 2 percent growth, and 4 percent unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, so that’s what—that’s what we did.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s what, together, the economy accomplished.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I don’t see any reason to think that we’re looking at, at a replay of the ’70s or anything like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, inflation—underlying inflation is, is, you know, still running in the 2s, with probably a little bit of a pickup associated with tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I, I don’t think we’re facing—I, I wouldn’t say we’re in, in a situation that’s remotely comparable to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, I—it’s not—it’s not appropriate for me to speculate on political ideas or, or fiscal policy, for that matter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I’m going to—I’m going to pass on that one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, since the very beginning, we’ve had kind of a placeholder—the staff has a placeholder of—range of—really a range of possible outcomes from tariffs, and from trade policy generally.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And they generally assume full retaliation in those.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so that’s, that’s kind of baked into the numbers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What happens—it will be complicated, and there will be some retaliation and some not and, and all that, but, ultimately, they’re trying to, with the placeholder, give us a broad sense of what this might look like.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This—when we know—when we actually know the specifics, we’ll be able to, to have still uncertain but, you know, better-informed forecasts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, so, yes, that’s in there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah, so we, we looked at pausing, and we looked at, at slowing, and, really, people came together very strongly behind slowing, not pausing, for a variety of reasons.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so people really came to be, you know, pretty strongly in favor of, of this move.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It slows down the path and probably lengthens it—you know, doubles it, effectively, by slowing it by half.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s, that’s—people thought that’s, that’s a good place to be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’ll, it’ll, you know, help us assure that this path is, is a smooth one as we get closer and closer to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s how that came about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, it was—it was actually—it was the, the TGA flows—Treasury General Account flows that got us thinking about this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But the more we thought about it, we came around to this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, and, you know, it, it is—yes, it was provoked.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The original discussion was provoked by that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I think what we came up with, though, was broader than that and different than it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It does address that issue, but it really is also—it fits in really nicely with our principles and our plans, and the things we’ve done before, and the things we’ve said we would do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s why I—you know, pretty, pretty strong support.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’d just say it’s, it’s nothing to do with monetary policy, nothing to do with the size of the balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s just kind of a commonsense adjustment as you get closer and closer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Let’s slow down a little bit again.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, that way, we’ll be more and more confident that we’re getting where we need to get.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You can take your time getting there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we’re shrinking the balance sheet every month, and we think that’s—we think it was a good play and, as I mentioned, well supported.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thanks very much.
